title: The Quiet Regiment
premise: In 1913 London, Wendell Crane drives for suffragist organizer Edith Marlowe and secretly reads every letter he delivers, memorizing what the movement cannot afford to lose. When a gaunt stranger arrives with letters in the handwriting of Alice Fenwick—a suffragist officially dead after a hunger strike—Wendell realizes Alice is alive, imprisoned in a private asylum, and her testimony could topple the officials who buried her. Smuggling her evidence past three checkpoints while evading both police and his own employer's cautious silence, Wendell must choose between invisibility and justice. The book ends with Alice's testimony published at last, Wendell exposed but unrepentant, and a quiet, hard-won love between him and Edith that survives the cost.
about_author: Astrid Hartwell is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing suffragette correspondence before turning to fiction. She writes from a converted coach house in Kent, where she keeps a wall of reproduced Edwardian letters pinned above her desk.

chapters.title: The Weight of Letters
chapters.summary: Wendell Crane's POV. We meet him measuring his world by what can be carried: parcels, secrets, Edith Marlowe's cause. He reads a letter meant only for Edith and files it away in memory. Emotional beat: the comfort of being invisible, and the first hairline crack of guilt in it.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Mews
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A rain-soaked stranger begs a word with Miss Marlowe and shows Wendell three letters—in unmistakable handwriting belonging to Alice Fenwick, declared dead eight months ago. Emotional beat: vertigo; the ground of Wendell's careful life tilts as the dead begin to speak.

chapters.title: What Edith Knew
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. She admits she suspected Alice survived Holloway's 'transfer' but chose strategy over truth. Wendell, stung, volunteers to carry the evidence himself. Emotional beat: love against duty—two people wanting the same justice through opposite doors.

chapters.title: The First Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He sews the letters into a spare tire and faces a suspicious constable at Blackfriars. A near-search is broken up by a suffragist protest staged precisely on cue. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into exhilaration—he is no longer invisible, and part of him likes it.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed the Order
chapters.summary: Antagonist POV: Inspector Rokeby, who arranged Alice's disappearance, learns a copy of her testimony exists. He begins pulling threads through the motor trade. Emotional beat: cold, bureaucratic menace—the law itself hunting justice outside it.

chapters.title: Letters to the Living
chapters.summary: Alice's POV, in asylum fragments interleaved with Wendell reading them aloud to Edith by lamplight. Her voice—fierce, funny, failing—binds the two conspirators closer. Emotional beat: grief and tenderness entwined; Wendell and Edith's first almost-touch.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Motor Works
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. His mechanic cousin, squeezed by Rokeby, tips off the second checkpoint. Wendell escapes through a coal yard, losing the tire—and nearly the letters—to a river. Emotional beat: betrayal by blood, and the discovery that he'd rather be caught than quit.

chapters.title: The Third Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Dual POV. With the original letters water-stained, Wendell memorizes every word and walks the final checkpoint carrying nothing but memory—while Edith creates a diversion that gets her arrested. Emotional beat: sacrifice; duty and love finally pointing the same direction.

chapters.title: Alice Fenwick, Alive
chapters.summary: Climax. Wendell reaches the press office as Rokeby closes in; Alice herself, smuggled out by sympathetic nurses, arrives to speak her own name before the reporters. Rokeby's arrest warrant lands on his own desk. Emotional beat: triumph earned at real price—Edith still in a cell, Wendell publicly named.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Resolution, Wendell's POV. Edith is released; Alice testifies before an inquiry; Rokeby's network unravels. Wendell, no longer a driver but now the movement's keeper of records, reads one letter openly—Edith's, addressed to him. Emotional beat: quiet joy; a man once invisible, finally seen.
